```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center")
library(catcheR)
library(knitr)

## Folder layout ------------------------------------------------------------
##   analysis_EB/
##     scratch/   <- all inputs (FASTQ, barcode CSVs, PIPseeker matrix)
##     Output/    <- everything this document writes
##
## Paths are built from params so the same file runs on any sample: point
## `analysis_dir` at the run folder and change `sample_name`.
SCRATCH <- file.path(params$analysis_dir, params$scratch)
OUT     <- file.path(params$analysis_dir, params$output)
dir.create(OUT, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

## knitr writes figure paths relative to the .Rmd, so embedding files that live
## in Output/ needs the relative path, not the absolute one.
show <- function(f, ext = "jpg") {
  p <- file.path(OUT, paste0(f, ".", ext))
  if (file.exists(p)) knitr::include_graphics(p) else invisible(NULL)
}
MAXR <- if (is.null(params$max_reads)) Inf else as.numeric(params$max_reads)
```

# The pipeline, and where this document sits in it

Four steps, in this order. Each one consumes what the previous produced, and
nothing here re-reads the FASTQ after the first step.

| # | step | reads | produces | needed by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `catcheR_pipcatch()` | the FASTQ pair and the barcode-to-gene CSVs | the `parsecatch` object (`.rds`), `complete_table_fin`, the 13 catcheR plots and the QC panels | every step below |
| 2 | `catcheR_pip_filtercatch()` | the object from 1 | `ValidCell` at the chosen thresholds, `cells_with_at_least_1_UCI.csv`, `new_cell_names.csv` | steps 3 and 4 |
| 3 | `catcheR_pip_nocatch()` | the object from 1 **and** the filter from 2 | the empty-vector cells, i.e. the unperturbed control set | step 4 (optional) |
| 4 | `catcheR_pip_seurat()` | the filter from 2, the empty set from 3, and PIPseeker's `matrix.mtx.gz` / `features.tsv.gz` / `barcodes.tsv.gz` | the Seurat object with `catcheR_status` on every cell | your downstream analysis |

**Why the order matters.** Step 3 needs step 2 because an "empty" cell is
defined as one that is *not* in the called set: without the filter there is
nothing to subtract from. Step 4 needs step 2 for the same reason and step 3
only if you want the controls labelled rather than left as `not_detected`.

**What can be repeated cheaply.** Steps 2 to 4 all act on the object, so
re-filtering at new thresholds costs seconds and never re-streams the reads.
Only step 1 is expensive.

## Where the files go

```
analysis_EB_PIP/
  scratch/                       <- inputs, plus the handoff copies below
  Output/
    pipcatch/                  <- step 1: this chemistry's own folder
      filtercatch_p15_u0_r2/     <- step 2, tagged with its thresholds
```

Step 1 nests under the chemistry name so that running the 10x or Parse
pipeline into the same `Output/` cannot overwrite these files - the 13 plots
carrying catcheR's own names have no chemistry in the filename. Step 2 adds a
folder named for its thresholds, so a second attempt at different values sits
beside the first instead of replacing it.

Three files are *inputs to a later step* rather than deliverables:
`cells_with_at_least_1_UCI.csv`, `new_cell_names.csv` and
`complete_table_fin_<sample>.csv`. With `to_scratch: true` they are copied into
`scratch/` as `<name>_pipcatch_<sample>.csv`, so two pipelines can
share one scratch without colliding. The originals stay in `Output/`.

## One trap in the thresholds

`UMI.count` and `percentage` exclude with a strict `>`, `min.cell.UMI` includes
with `>=`. So `UMI.count = 1` keeps pairs of **two or more** UMIs, a UCI at
exactly 15% does **not** pass `percentage = 15`, and a cell with exactly 20
cassette UMIs **does** pass `min.cell.UMI = 20`. PIPseq has no deduplicable molecular index, so every count here is
**reads**, not molecules: per-cell totals top out around ten and a floor tuned
for a UMI-counted library would exclude every cell. That is why this document
leaves `UMI.count = 0` and no floor.

# Inputs

Everything the run needs sits in `scratch/`. The chunk below is a guard: it
fails loudly here rather than halfway through a 20 minute stream.

```{r inputs}
need <- c(params$fastq_r1, params$fastq_r2, params$barcodes_genes)
inv  <- data.frame(
  file   = need,
  exists = file.exists(file.path(SCRATCH, need)),
  size_MB = round(file.size(file.path(SCRATCH, need)) / 1024^2, 1)
)
stopifnot(all(inv$exists))
kable(inv, caption = sprintf("Inputs found in %s", SCRATCH))
```

Two barcode-to-gene CSVs are passed because the two shRNA libraries were pooled
before loading. `catcheR_pipcatch()` merges them, tags every construct with the
set it came from, and resolves each file's orientation on its own — one of these
two is reverse-complemented relative to the other, and the function reports which.

# Extraction and first-stage QC

One pass over the read pair. This is the only expensive step (roughly 7 minutes
for an 18 M pair library), so the chunk is cached: re-knitting to adjust a plot
or a threshold does not re-read the FASTQ.

Set `max_reads` in the YAML header to a few million for a fast dry run; leave it
empty (`~`) to use every read.

```{r pipcatch, cache=TRUE}
res <- catcheR_pipcatch(
  folder         = SCRATCH,
  fastq.read1    = params$fastq_r1,
  fastq.read2    = params$fastq_r2,
  barcodes.genes = params$barcodes_genes,
  set.names      = params$set_names,
  set.sizes      = as.integer(params$set_sizes),
  # PIPseeker's own called-cell list. Supplying it is what unlocks the panels
  # whose denominator is "cells the platform called" rather than "barcodes we
  # happened to see" - the latter overstates coverage severalfold.
  called.cells   = file.path(SCRATCH, paste0(params$gex_prefix, ".barcodes.tsv.gz")),
  output_dir     = OUT,
  sample_name    = params$sample_name,
  percentage     = params$percentage,
  ratio          = params$ratio,
  UMI.count      = params$umi_count,
  jitter         = params$jitter,
  max.reads      = MAXR,
  verbose        = FALSE
)
# The entry point nests its outputs one level down, under the chemistry name,
# so another pipeline writing into the same Output/ cannot overwrite these.
# Take the path from the object rather than rebuilding it here.
OUT <- res$output_dir
res
```

## What each read turned out to be

The enrichment PCR is the bottleneck in this library, so it is worth reading
this table before anything else: it says how much of the sequencing actually
carried the cassette.

```{r read-classes}
kable(res$read_class, caption = "Read fates")
```

## Threshold suggestions

`catcheR` offers two automatic estimators for the `UMIxUCI` cut. Both are
reported; neither is applied unless you pass it to `UMI.count`.

At this depth the deliberate choice is **`UMI.count = 0`** — the distribution is
dominated by single-read (cell, UCI) pairs, so any positive threshold discards
most of the data. More sequencing, not a cleverer threshold, is the fix.

```{r thresholds}
thr <- res$thresholds
kable(data.frame(
  quantity = c("(cell, UCI) pairs", "single-read pairs", "% single-read",
               'mode = "noise" would pick', 'mode = "bimodal" would pick',
               "applied (UMI.count)"),
  value    = c(thr$pairs, thr$singletons, round(thr$pct_singletons, 1),
               thr$noise, thr$bimodal, params$umi_count)
), caption = "Threshold estimators (NA = the estimator found nothing to cut on)")
```

## The seven first-stage plots

Written to `Output/` as both `.jpg` and `.pdf`, under the same file names
`catcheR_10Xcatch` uses.

```{r stage1-barcode, fig.cap="barcode_distribution — reads per construct, filled by gene"}
show("barcode_distribution")
```

```{r stage1-gene, fig.cap="gene_distribution — reads per target gene"}
show("gene_distribution")
```

```{r stage1-umixuci, fig.cap="UMIxUCI — reads per (cell, UCI) pair"}
show("UMIxUCI")
```

The zoomed version of the same histogram clips the singleton peak so the tail is
readable. Its file name carries the window that was used, and with `zoom.x` and
`zoom.y` left at `NULL` that window is derived from the data.

```{r stage1-zoom, fig.cap="UMIxUCI zoomed — singleton peak clipped"}
zf <- list.files(OUT, pattern = "^UMIxUCI_[0-9]+_[0-9]+\\.jpg$")
if (length(zf)) knitr::include_graphics(file.path(OUT, zf[1]))
```

```{r stage1-ucixcell, fig.cap="UCIxcell — distinct UCIs per cell barcode"}
show("UCIxcell")
```

```{r stage1-pct, fig.cap="percentage_of_UMIxUCI_dist — share of a cell's reads held by each UCI"}
show("percentage_of_UMIxUCI_dist")
```

```{r stage1-2d, fig.cap="2D_percentage_of_UMIxUCI_UMI_count — the plane the filter works in"}
show("2D_percentage_of_UMIxUCI_UMI_count")
```

A note on that last panel. `catcheR` draws it with `geom_count()`, sizing each
marker by how many pairs share a coordinate — the right geometry at 10X depth,
where the axes are near-continuous. Here `UMIxUCI` takes a handful of integer
values and the percentage only simple fractions, so thousands of pairs land on a
few dozen coordinates and `geom_count()` collapses into three or four huge
bubbles. With `jitter = "auto"` the function detects that and spreads the points
instead. The data plotted is identical; force either geometry with
`jitter = TRUE` / `jitter = FALSE`.

```{r jitter-check}
data.frame(
  pairs       = nrow(res$tab),
  coordinates = nrow(unique(res$tab[, c("UMIpercentagexUCI", "UMIxUCI")])),
  jittered    = catcheR:::.cat_jitter_on(res$tab, params$jitter)
)
```

# Cell filtering

`catcheR_pip_filtercatch()` re-applies the thresholds without re-reading the
FASTQ, writes `cells_with_at_least_1_UCI.csv` and `new_cell_names.csv`, and
regenerates the six second-stage plots at the refined settings.

```{r filtercatch}
flt <- catcheR_pip_filtercatch(res,
  # the files a later step reads are copied into scratch/, renamed with the
  # chemistry and the sample, so several pipelines can share one scratch
  to.scratch   = if (isTRUE(params$to_scratch)) SCRATCH else NULL,
                               UMI.count  = params$umi_count,
                               percentage = params$percentage,
                               ratio      = params$ratio,
                               output_dir = OUT,
                               jitter     = params$jitter,
                               verbose    = FALSE)
kable(flt$filter_returns, caption = "ValidCell count across candidate thresholds")
```

```{r stage2-thr, fig.cap="2D_percentage_of_UMIxUCI_UMI_count_thresholds"}
show("2D_percentage_of_UMIxUCI_UMI_count_thresholds")
```

```{r stage2-true, fig.cap="true_UCIxcell — cells by number of UCIs passing the filter"}
show("true_UCIxcell")
```

```{r stage2-truefalse, fig.cap="2D_percentage_of_UMIxUCI_UMI_count_trueorfalse"}
show("2D_percentage_of_UMIxUCI_UMI_count_trueorfalse")
```

```{r stage2-clones, fig.cap="cellsxclone — cells per clone (UCI)"}
show("cellsxclone")
```

```{r stage2-clones-log, fig.cap="cellsxclone_log10"}
show("cellsxclone_log10")
```

```{r stage2-valid, fig.cap="2D_percentage_of_UMIxUCI_UMI_count_ValidCells"}
show("2D_percentage_of_UMIxUCI_UMI_count_ValidCells")
```

# Unperturbed cells

Cells carrying the empty vector. Read the printed note: at low depth the
absence of a cassette read is far more often a sampling failure than a real
empty cell, and the function says so rather than handing back a control set it
cannot support.

```{r nocatch}
noc <- catcheR_pip_nocatch(res, filtered = flt, threshold = 0,
                           output_dir = OUT, verbose = TRUE)
```

# PIPseq-specific panels

These six have no `catcheR_10Xcatch` equivalent — they exist because the
PIPseq cell barcode has to be parsed out of read 1 rather than sliced at a fixed
offset, which makes the per-cell denominators and the no-call fates worth
showing explicitly.

```{r pip-detect, fig.cap="Cell detection: how many barcodes survive each step"}
show("pipcatch_cell_detection", "png")
```

```{r pip-nocall, fig.cap="What the cells without a call actually contain"}
show("pipcatch_nocall_fates", "png")
```

```{r pip-clone, fig.cap="Constructs detected and clones per construct"}
show("pipcatch_shRNA_clone_matrix", "png")
```

```{r pip-dist, fig.cap="Barcode and gene distributions, both libraries"}
show("pipcatch_QC_distributions", "png")
```

```{r pip-thr, fig.cap="Threshold diagnostics as produced by the extraction step"}
show("pipcatch_QC_thresholds", "png")
```

```{r pip-fthr, fig.cap="The same diagnostics recomputed at the refined thresholds"}
show("pipcatch_filtercatch_thresholds", "png")
```

## Judged against the cells PIPseeker actually called

Everything above counts every barcode the enrichment library produced, ambient
included. The honest denominator is PIPseeker's own cell list.

```{r called-comp, fig.cap="Clone composition of the called cells"}
show("pipcatch_called_composition", "png")
```

```{r called-floor, fig.cap="The read-floor panel restricted to called cells"}
show("pipcatch_UCI_per_cell_called", "png")
```

```{r called-yield, fig.cap="Yield against expected wrong calls"}
show("pipcatch_yield_vs_error", "png")
```

# Join to the expression matrix

Optional, and skipped automatically when the PIPseeker files are not in
`scratch/`. PIPseeker writes `barcodes.tsv.gz` as the same 28 nt concatenated
four-tier barcode that `pipcatch` extracts, so the join is a plain string match
— the function warns if it ever sees a different width.

Note the cell counts here, not the ones above: dividing by *called* cells is the
honest denominator, and a fraction of the calls fall on ambient barcodes that
PIPseeker never called as cells.

```{r seurat}
gex <- file.path(SCRATCH, paste0(params$gex_prefix,
                                 c(".matrix.mtx.gz", ".features.tsv.gz", ".barcodes.tsv.gz")))
if (all(file.exists(gex))) {
  obj <- catcheR_pip_seurat(res, filtered = flt, empty = noc,
                            mtx = gex[1], features = gex[2], cells = gex[3],
                            sample_id = params$sample_name,
                            project   = params$sample_name,
                            rename = TRUE, subset.valid = TRUE,
                            output_dir = OUT, verbose = TRUE)
} else {
  message("PIPseeker matrix not found in scratch/ - skipping the join.")
}
```

When you scale this to several samples, attach the metadata to each object
*before* `merge(..., add.cell.ids = ...)`. The merge prefixes every barcode with
the sample id, after which the 28 nt key no longer matches.
